# Local restaurant supply simulation

This lab follows a household meal request through ingredient sourcing, cooking,
and courier delivery in the fictional 32×32 city. The household, restaurant, and
market workers run deterministic local rules. No model account, voice service,
provider key, or paid inference is required. The simulated phone conversations
are text records and queue messages; they do not place telephone calls.

The starting city contains 128 synthetic households, seven restaurants, and three
ingredient markets. Its homes come from the existing urban fixture. Each
restaurant initially serves one recipe from `data/meal-snapshot.json`:

| Recipe ID | Meal |
| --- | --- |
| `pizza` | Pizza |
| `kebab` | Kebab |
| `hamburgers` | Hamburgers |
| `steak-frites` | Steak frites |
| `sushi` | Sushi |
| `soups` | Soups |
| `salads` | Salads |

`market-a`, `market-b`, and `market-c` occupy the map nodes of `store-1`,
`store-5`, and `store-10`. Their ingredient role belongs to this simulation;
the older shop categories do not define their permissions here.

## Editable blueprint and frozen run

The blueprint is the saved configuration for the next run. Saving a draft changes
that blueprint and its revision. Starting a run freezes the selected configuration,
its canonical SHA-256 digest, the entity definitions, opening stock, and agent
definitions for that run. Later blueprint edits do not rewrite running or saved
orders, inventory, identities, or evidence. A revision check prevents a stale editor
from silently replacing a newer blueprint.

An entity is a household, restaurant, or market with its own ID and node. Its
editable definition includes:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `id`, `name`, `kind`, `node` | Stable reference, display name, one fixed entity kind, and grid node 0–1023 |
| `recipe_ids` | Restaurant menu or household meal preferences; markets have no prepared-meal menu |
| `opening_hours` | Local daily availability as `{ "start": 11, "end": 23 }` |
| `order_hours` | Household call windows, initially lunch 12–14 and dinner 19–21 |
| `allow_substitutions` | Whether the household may approve a proposed ingredient alternative |
| `excluded_ingredients` | Canonical ingredient IDs the household excludes |
| `agent` | Optional complete agent definition for this entity; `null` inherits its role template |
| `opening_stock` | Restaurant/market overrides by canonical ingredient ID, in whole grams, millilitres or pieces; 0–100000 per ingredient |

Hours are integer local hours with an inclusive start and exclusive end. `0–24`
means all day; `23–2` continues through midnight. Equal start and end are rejected.
Definitions require unique entity IDs, canonical recipe and ingredient IDs, and at
least one household, restaurant, and market. The city admits at most 160 entities.

The `agents` object has exactly three templates: `household`, `restaurant`, and
`market`. Each has `display_name`, `soul`, `latency_seconds`, `limits`, and `search`. A template
edit applies to entities that inherit that template in the next run. An entity
override applies only to that entity. Removing the override restores inheritance.

Display names and SOUL text are stored and versioned descriptions. The present
rules do not ask a model to interpret SOUL text. Timing and budget fields have
executable effects; editing a description does not add a decision procedure or
grant permissions. Entity kind determines the role, and the server owns its tools,
topics, identity, and recipients. Unknown fields and attempted tool or role
injection are rejected by the strict definition models.

## Finite demand and timing controls

| Setting | Default | Accepted range |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `seed` | 42 | 0–2³¹−1 |
| `duration_minutes` | 120 | 15–1440 |
| `start_hour` | 11 | 0–23 |
| `playback_seconds` | 60 | 0–120 |
| `calls_per_household` | 1 | 0–3 |
| `communication_latency_seconds` | 5 | 0–120 |
| `supplier_delay_seconds` | 60 | 0–1800 |
| `restaurant_stock_servings` | 0 | 0–10 |
| `market_stock_servings` | 3 | 0–20 |
| `fleet_couriers` | 6 | 1–16 |

Each household has an independent seeded random sequence for its calls. The
scheduler intersects its order windows with its own availability and the opening
hours of restaurants offering a preferred meal. It produces at most **64 calls
for the whole run**, even when more households are configured. The 128 homes are
potential participants rather than a promise of 128 calls. Zero calls is valid.

Each scheduled call includes a stable order ID, household, restaurant, meal,
quantity one, simulated arrival time, delivery deadline, customer node, and a
human-readable request transcript. The deadline is two simulated hours after
the call. Future schedules belong to the operator; they do not give agents
advance knowledge of future orders.

Communication latency and an entity's resolved agent latency are additive. With
both defaults set to five, a normal communication handoff takes ten simulated
seconds. They change queue due times rather than making worker threads sleep.
Playback controls the pace at which the operator watches the simulation; it does
not change ingredient quantities, message order, or road traversal rules.

Supplier delay models the wait between reservation and dispatch. The ingredient
arrival is a later queued transition. Stock promised by a supplier is not usable
in the restaurant until that arrival commits. This slice does not simulate a
separate supplier vehicle moving along the map. The last mile uses the existing
dispatcher and courier system on directed city streets.

## Meal and ingredient lifecycle

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    H[Household] -->|queued meal call| R[Restaurant]
    R -->|ingredient request| M[Nearest market]
    M -->|shortage forwarding| N[Another market]
    M -->|reserved then arrived| R
    N -->|reserved then arrived| R
    R -->|substitution offer| H
    H -->|explicit approval| R
    R -->|cook from arrived stock| D[Dispatcher and courier]
    D -->|confirmed delivery| H
```

1. A due household intent queues a call to its selected restaurant. The
   restaurant checks that it offers the requested recipe and is open when the
   call is handled.
2. The restaurant reserves available ingredients from its own pantry and creates
   separate requests for shortages. It sends each request to a selected nearby
   market. The recipe and its quantities come from the validated meal snapshot.
3. A market checks its own unreserved stock for the requested ingredient and
   canonical unit. A full available quantity is reserved atomically. A shortage
   forwards the request to another unvisited market; the visited list prevents
   loops and the hop bound ends an unsuccessful search.
4. A reservation schedules transfer and subsequent arrival. The market's physical
   stock decreases on dispatch; the restaurant receives and reserves the actual
   ingredient on arrival. The order cannot cook from a reservation, an ETA, or an
   in-transit promise alone.
5. When sourcing fails, a fixed substitution table may offer a compatible-unit
   alternative. Exclusions still apply. The offer goes to the actual household
   as an event, and its reply must approve the proposal before the restaurant
   sources the alternative. Declining, an unsafe alternative, exhausted suppliers,
   or deadline expiry fails the order and releases applicable reservations.
6. Cooking consumes the restaurant's reserved physical allocations once, creates
   a ready delivery job, and queues the dispatcher handoff. Delivery becomes
   complete only after the existing courier workflow reports delivery.

The fixed alternatives and exclusion checks are synthetic business rules. They
are not a nutritional, allergy, or medical assessment. Editing SOUL text cannot
invent an alternative or bypass consent.

Stock quantities retain their canonical units: grams (`g`), millilitres (`ml`),
or count (`piece`). The code rejects unit mismatches instead of treating a piece,
gram, and millilitre as interchangeable. Stock uses the indexed tuple
`(run_id, owner, ingredient)` as its primary key; order and request indexes cover
household, restaurant, market, and order lookups. Finding a row is a database
operation. The scenario does not need semantic search or a model to look up
inventory.

## Agent authority and queue boundary

Every supply entity gets a separate temporary PostgreSQL login. Its authenticated
binding fixes the run, entity namespace, role definition hash, private memory,
and durable budget. Agents receive scoped tools rather than the operator's
database connection or whole-city snapshot.

| Role | Observations and actions |
| --- | --- |
| Household | Its own meal orders and requests; initiate a call, approve or decline an offered substitution, observe delivery |
| Restaurant | Its own orders, ingredient requests, and pantry; reserve, source, receive, cook, and queue the delivery handoff |
| Market | Requests currently assigned to that market and its own stock; reserve, transfer, or forward to another permitted supplier |

The four tools used by the local policy are `supply.read`, `supply.command`,
`memory.read`, and `memory.write`. A fifth capability, `supply.search`, is available
through the authenticated leased-message endpoint for restaurant and market agents.
The command validates the actor's current event lease and executes
one supported domain transition. Its stock mutations, outgoing messages, and
audit fact share a transaction. The tool has no editable recipient, tool list,
raw SQL, filesystem, arbitrary network, or code execution argument. Supply roles
do not receive the general `queue.publish` capability.

A market projection omits household identity, preferences, full menu, recipe, and
restaurant pantry. Typed private memory is bound to that identity's current leased
order; markets are further restricted to the current ingredient request. The
operator inspector can inspect each identity for debugging; that broader human
view is not inserted into a market's context.

Role-specific accepted and emitted topics, destination checks, row security,
lease tokens, deduplication keys, retries, and durable budgets remain enforced.
The domain outbox checks that the destination has a binding that accepts its
topic. A repeated committed event returns its earlier result rather than
reserving or consuming stock twice. Supplier forwarding carries a bounded visited
list rather than recursively calling other agents.

Default supply-agent limits are 500 event attempts, five tool slots per event,
2,000 tool calls per run, 64 memory entries, and 16,384 memory bytes. Editable
limits stay inside `RoleLimits` ceilings. Four slots serve the normal policy and
one permits an optional search during the same event. The supply fleet has a
separate frozen profile: dispatcher 333 events/six slots, courier 333 events/five
slots, each with 2,000 tools, 100 memory entries and 65,536 memory bytes. This
profile retains the existing dispatch/courier permissions. Ordinary meal policies
make zero model calls. Optional search has its own durable admission ledger.
The trusted operator, server code, and
database administrator remain outside the agent sandbox boundary.

## Operator API and local operation

The HTTP interface is the local human operator surface. Agent-to-agent messages
use the authenticated queue and domain commands described above. An agent
inspection URL does not issue agent credentials or authorize queue publication.

Start the existing local stack from Bash:

```sh
make up
```

Open [the restaurant lab](http://localhost:8010/restaurant-lab), or choose
Restaurants in the shared navigation. Search or filter the agent roster, then
select a restaurant, supermarket or household to edit its next-run
definition or inspect its frozen stock, orders, memory and budget. Advanced JSON
supports per-ingredient opening stock and per-entity or shared agent definitions.

Click the **Orders** metric to open all orders for the current run, independent of
the selected agent. Each order expands into its customer call, ingredient requests,
complete timeline, queued messages and agent memory. The order opens with a chat:
stable fictional agent names, entity/role labels, simulation timestamps, delivery
receipts and readable memory changes. Raw queue evidence remains collapsed.
Section buttons jump between conversation, steps and memory; expanded orders stay
open during live updates. Future calls remain listed as scheduled before arrival.

The run URL accepts `?run=<run UUID>` so a frozen conversation can be reopened.
New runs update that URL. System scheduling and world events are compact
disclosures; customer and agent messages display as chat bubbles. A queue ACK
without an agent decision is labeled explicitly, rather than inventing a receipt
time or memory change. Memory snapshots without a prior baseline are also labeled.

Conversation verification on 2026-10-27: 32 focused runtime, API, presentation and
supply tests passed. After correcting world-event sender attribution, the 11
presentation/API checks passed again. Ruff, JavaScript syntax and mypy (35 source
files) passed. Browser checks covered the existing 64-order run, persistent order
expansion across entity selection, keyboard collapse, legacy memory labels and a
fresh two-order run with named agents and visible before/after memory changes.
Both fresh meals delivered; replay matched and stock conservation, nonnegative
stock and canonical units passed. The provider remained disabled. No browser
console errors or horizontal overflow were observed at the default viewport.

See [memory architecture and next steps](AGENT-MEMORY.md) for enterprise references
and the distinction between current working records and proposed long-term recall.

The evidence download fetches the complete server
bundle rather than exporting only the dashboard's recent window.

From 2026-10-27, successful memory writes are retained in the same transaction as
the decision and event acknowledgement. The order inspector can show those actual
writes after live memory expires. Older runs show retained memory and recorded
decision context, with an explicit notice when historical writes are unavailable.
Typed writes append revisions with source events, observation time and expiry.
The operator reconstructs before/after changes from that ledger; agent write
receipts do not disclose previous bodies. The memory section shows the actual
fact IDs and revisions recalled for each decision. Live recall excludes other
roles, orders, ingredient requests, expired facts and superseded revisions.
The history belongs to the trusted operator view and is unavailable through agent
table access or the retired broad memory endpoint.

The default Compose configuration binds the application to loopback, sets
`LLM_PROVIDER=disabled`, and uses local services. No Jev, telephony, speech,
or cloud model is enabled by starting a supply run.

| Endpoint | Boundary |
| --- | --- |
| `GET/PUT /api/supply/blueprint` | Trusted local operator; `PUT` requires `If-Match` revision |
| `POST /api/supply/runs` | Freeze the saved revision and start a local run |
| `GET /api/supply/runs/{run}` | Operator's entities, stock, orders, queue and metrics |
| `GET /api/supply/runs/{run}/orders/{order}` | Complete single-order events, facts, decisions, requests and recorded memory; no recent-window truncation |
| `GET /api/supply/runs/{run}/agents/{agent}` | Operator inspection of one agent's memory, definition and decisions |
| `POST .../agents/{agent}/channel` | Requires a separately configured `DELIVERY_OPERATOR_KEY` in `X-Operator-Key`; disabled by default |
| `POST .../agents/{agent}/claim` | Bearer token bound to this run and agent; claims only its accepted messages |
| `POST .../agents/{agent}/calls` | Process an owned household intent; the command queues its restaurant call |
| `POST .../agents/{agent}/messages` | Process the exact owned event ID, lease token and attempt; arbitrary payloads/recipients are rejected |
| `POST .../agents/{agent}/search` | Same lease envelope plus `query` and `mode`; fresh own-stock observations only |
| `POST .../agents/{agent}/memory/recall` | Bearer token + current event lease; typed facts for own role/order/request, expiry and result bounds |
| `GET .../agents/{agent}/memory` | Retired (410); broad namespace recall is unavailable |
| `GET .../entities/{entity}/search?query=...` | Operator's free local ingredient search, available after a run finishes |
| `GET .../replay`, `GET .../evidence` | Operator verification and complete JSON bundle |

Agent IDs use `household:<entity>`, `restaurant:<entity>` and `market:<entity>`.
Channels expire after an hour and are removed when the run ends. External workers
and the local controller compete through queue leases, not direct RPC. Calls are
typed, scripted meal intents; this is not speech recognition or telephone service.
The local operator HTTP surface is trusted and intentionally broader than agent
context. It is not a public multi-tenant authorization system. Supply endpoints
reject unknown hosts and cross-origin mutations.

Agent isolation here constrains registered tools, authenticated SQL sessions and
the scoped agent endpoints. It does not sandbox hostile Python code, host network
access or an operating-system user who can access the trusted operator surface.
Untrusted executable workers would need a separate process/container and network
policy before the operator UI could share a host with them safely.

## Audit and replay

Supply commands append ordered facts with their actor, order, event topic,
simulated time, parent hash, fact hash, result, transactional outbox, and domain
after-images. The opening snapshot and frozen definitions establish the starting
state. Audit projections belong to operator evidence and are not returned as
agent context.

Delivery-job inserts and changed updates also append after-images in the same
database transaction, including movement and late delivery after an order has
failed its deadline. Those are trusted world/dispatcher observations with a null
message-event ID; they are not fabricated agent messages. Unchanged updates add no
fact. Agent roles cannot call the trigger helper or write the ledger directly.

The hash chain provides a consistency check over the recorded sequence. It does
not prove authenticity against an administrator who can rewrite the database.
Replay validation should be read together with its reported projection and
invariant results; it is not a claim of externally verified execution or model
determinism.

Replay applies recorded after-images to opening state and compares stock, orders,
requests, allocations and delivery jobs with the persisted projections. It does
not rerun agents or query a provider. The observation window ends at demand duration
plus two simulated hours; unfinished orders and open delivery jobs are reported,
not counted as delivered. A late physical delivery remains distinct from meeting
the meal deadline. Supplier distance currently uses public Euclidean coordinates;
last-mile courier routes use the directed road graph.

Inventory conservation checks each ingredient independently: opening physical
stock equals closing physical stock plus cooked consumption plus quantities still
in supplier transit. Reserved units remain part of physical on-hand stock.
The live snapshot limits its event window to 1,000 messages and fact window to 100;
evidence export includes every message, decision, fact and search audit without
channel credentials or event lease tokens. A capture made while the run is active
is marked `live_capture`; use a finished run for final evidence.

## Jev and future decision adapters

TypeSafe describes Jev as a model for typed questions over supplied state,
including choice, score, and truth-like responses. Its documented patterns include
intent routing and confidence-gated routing. Those are possible decision adapters
around this system's scoped business facts; Jev does not supply this project's
inventory database, search indexes, queue, or stock authority.
Sources: [TypeSafe introduction](https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction),
[TypeSafe patterns](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns).

The local baseline household, restaurant, and market policies use deterministic
rules with zero model calls. Optional Jev-assisted search must be configured
separately; ordinary stock lookup and the baseline run require no network calls.
A decision adapter needs bounded questions,
allowlisted typed answers, role-scoped facts, measured latency and cost, durable
per-role budgets, and a tested confidence or failure fallback to local rules.
It must pass the same stock, consent, recipient, and lease validation. Voice
recognition, generated speech, and real phone calls would each require a separate
adapter and evaluation; none are implied by the current text transcripts.

### Implemented search adapter

The adapter follows the existing Scrapmarket retrieval/review/cache pattern using
only this project's synthetic ingredient catalogue:

1. Normalize English/Spanish names and retrieve a bounded local candidate set
   (at most 60, with at most eight per vendor when a vendor is provided).
2. Optionally review relevance with Jev in batches of eight, using typed
   `yes/no/uncertain` choices and fixed answer IDs. Query text and candidate
   IDs/names/units are untrusted data. Owner IDs, stock quantities, customer facts,
   recipes and memory are not automatically included in provider payloads. The
   explicit caller's search text is transmitted when paid mode is selected.
3. Cache only successful yes/no relevance answers for 24 hours, keyed by the
   run/agent namespace, model, prompt, normalized query and catalogue fingerprint.
   Uncertain answers and failures are not cached. Confident negatives remain
   negative; fallback must be explicit.
4. Read availability afresh after review. A cached relevance match never caches
   stock or authorizes a reservation.

Network work holds no inventory locks or open agent transaction. Requests have
fixed HTTPS origin, no redirects, no automatic retries, bounded responses,
five-second HTTP timeouts and a 15-second overall review deadline. Model/version,
answer IDs and usage are validated. Every provider attempt reserves its call and
input-token allowance in a committed transaction before sending. Failures, unknown
usage and crashes retain that reservation; actual usage is recorded separately.
This is admission accounting, not a currency-price estimate or proof that a remote
provider billed exactly that amount.

Paid search needs **all** of these gates:

- Frozen agent `search` settings with `provider: "jev"`, `calls_limit` 1–8 and
  positive `input_tokens_limit` up to 51200. The default is local, zero calls/tokens.
- Server opt-in `DELIVERY_JEV_ENABLED=1`, an explicit `TYPESAFE_MODEL` version and
  `TYPESAFE_API_KEY`.
- A valid scoped agent channel, active incoming-message lease and durable tool slot.

Store credentials directly in ignored `.env.jev`, never in a blueprint, browser,
evidence bundle or chat. The optional `compose.jev.yaml` reads that file and pins
`jev-1.14.0` unless explicitly overridden. It also requires an operator key set in
the shell. Base Compose does not load this file or enable Jev. No GCP resources
are involved in this adapter.

```sh
# After privately setting a fresh key in .env.jev and DELIVERY_OPERATOR_KEY:
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.jev.yaml up -d --no-deps app
# Return to the free city baseline:
docker compose -f compose.yaml up -d --no-deps app
```

The reviewed city policies stay deterministic even when search is enabled. Search
is an optional authenticated decision tool, not an autonomous model-controlled
inventory writer. Live Jev verification remains pending; provider tests use
injected responses rather than a real credential.

## Verification

Verified locally on 2026-10-26. The complete suite passed **271 tests**. Subsequent
targeted checks passed all ten search service cases (including a new expired-review
lease regression), plus seven API/controller cases after the full-history export,
ingress optimization and conservation checks. Ruff passed and mypy passed all
34 source modules. All 31 definition tests also passed after freezing empty stock
overrides. Provider responses were injected; no live Jev request was sent.

The full seed-42 city admitted 64 meal calls and handled 1,762 events with zero
dead letters and zero model calls. Its 1,791 facts replayed to matching stock,
order, request, allocation and delivery-job projections. All inventory invariants
passed. This is a development receipt, not a pinned performance benchmark.

The intentionally constrained baseline delivered seven meals on time. Thirty-three
orders had no safe available ingredient alternative; 24 missed their meal deadline.
At the observation limit, 21 physical delivery jobs remained open and three
completed deliveries were late. Those outcomes are retained in metrics rather than
being counted as successful meal service. Better stock/courier settings and a
deadline-aware planner are separate improvements to evaluate.

A separate browser smoke delivered both meals, inspected scoped restaurant memory,
searched a market's stock locally, and verified all five replay projections. The
final UI check confirmed working navigation and call transcripts, no console
errors, and no overflow at 390 pixels. The original 138-entity blueprint was restored.

The [machine-readable local receipt](evidence/restaurant-supply-local.json) records
the results, discovered regressions, limits and remaining work. Host/process crash
supervision, real speech, interpreted model souls, broader substitutions, agent
topology comparisons and live-provider benchmarks remain future work.

# Local basket-to-delivery slice

This document describes the preserved first delivery slice and its regression
backend. The Delivery grid UI is retired and `/delivery-lab` redirects to Operations.
Saved legacy runs remain available through the delivery APIs. See also the
[expanded fleet recovery scenario](FLEET-RECOVERY.md).
The existing `/lab` last-unit/crash/delayed-supply scenario remains available.
Both use the same local factory, permissions, scoped tools, private memory,
durable budgets and fenced event-processing transaction.

```sh
docker compose exec -T app delivery delivery-demo
```

This runs a synthetic one-item basket on the 10×10 city, exports an evidence bundle
to ignored `artifacts/delivery-<run>.json`, and makes no model or provider calls.
Recorded evidence includes role boundaries, budgets, decision inputs, queue lineage
and consistent checkpoints. It is not a complete replay engine.

## Queue-only lifecycle

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    S[Scenario] -->|basket.requested| Q[(Postgres queue)]
    Q --> I[Inventory: own store]
    I -->|basket.reserved| Q
    Q --> F[Fulfillment: own store]
    F -->|basket.ready| Q
    Q --> D[Dispatcher: run fleet]
    D -->|delivery.assigned| Q
    W[Trusted physical world] -->|delivery.arrived| Q
    D -->|delivery.completed| Q
```

1. Inventory reserves one confirmed unit and emits an opaque basket reference.
2. Fulfillment validates the live own-store reservation, decrements on-hand and
   reserved stock together, writes one ledger movement and creates a ready job.
   The reservation becomes `picked`; repeated picking has no second effect.
3. Dispatch reads the logistics projection and selects an available bike. It
   plans connected roads from the courier's node through the store to the customer.
   The command independently validates endpoints, every directed edge and travel
   time, and atomically claims the courier. Concurrent jobs cannot claim one bike.
4. The world engine advances simulation time and the courier along those edges.
   It marks collection/in-transit/arrival and publishes `delivery.arrived`, linked
   to the assignment event. Agents cannot move the clock or manufacture arrival.
5. Dispatch confirms delivery only after authoritative arrival, releases the
   courier, marks the basket delivered and publishes the final queued result.

For seed 42, the bike travels from depot node 22 through pickup node 2 to customer
node 88. Collection occurs at simulation second 138 and arrival at second 1,016.
The UI uses individual edge travel times when placing the courier.

## Enforced role boundaries

| Identity | Permitted facts and actions | Denied access |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `inventory:store-N` | Own-store stock, reservations, replenishment and catalogue projection | Fulfillment commands, dispatch commands and other store/run state |
| `fulfillment:store-N` | Own reserved basket's SKU, quantity, expiry and picking status; atomic pick; queued ready handoff | Raw stock/catalogue/world/fleet tables, other stores, route assignment and delivery confirmation |
| `dispatcher:fleet` | This run's opaque ready jobs, road graph and courier availability; assign and confirm after arrival | Product identities, quantities, prices, stock, picking and fulfillment memory |

Five inventory and five fulfillment identities plus one dispatcher are provisioned
through separate non-superuser logins. Only three perform work in this small demo;
the other identities make the boundaries inspectable. Role namespaces are distinct
keys in the existing binding/budget/memory tables: inventory retains `store-N`,
fulfillment uses `fulfillment:store-N`, and dispatch uses `dispatcher:fleet`.

New roles have no direct table grants on inventory, fulfillment jobs or fleet.
Fixed security-definer projections/commands bind access to authenticated identity;
each command has role-specific execution grants. Event row security limits incoming
topics and destinations, and allows inspection of the identity's own outgoing
handoffs. Trusted destination rules route handoffs; policies cannot choose arbitrary
agents or stores. All messages retain the basket trace and parent event ID.

Definitions in `config/agents/{inventory,fulfillment,dispatcher}` are frozen per
run. JSON and soul text cannot grant another role's tools. Private expiring memory
and budget tickets use the same runtime as inventory. Default agent caps remain
100 attempts, eight slots per attempt, 400 slots per run and zero model spend;
the aggregate run cap remains 500 attempts and 2,000 slots.

The operator API/UI, fixed Python implementations and host are trusted, as documented
in [the foundation](AGENT-FOUNDATION.md). This is not an arbitrary-code sandbox.

## Verification and limits

The full Linux suite passes 76 tests, including nine new lifecycle/permission tests;
an additional operator API contract test passes separately. Ruff and mypy pass.
Chrome checks cover delivered stock, 100 nodes/360 roads, role boundaries, evidence
download, completed-run reload and desktop/mobile layout.

Tests include expired reservations, rollback of picking and its outgoing handoff
together, retry without duplicate consumption, forbidden direct table reads,
cross-store fulfillment denial, role switching, forged producers/destinations,
budget modification, hidden product data in dispatch, fabricated arrival,
disconnected routes and concurrent courier claims. Existing actual worker-crash
and Madrid regressions continue to pass.

This is a single-item, single-courier happy-path delivery slice. Continuous worker
supervision, controller restart recovery, cancellations/returns, arbitrary basket
expiry scheduling, cargo/energy constraints, traffic disruptions, multi-basket
dispatch waiting, architecture comparisons and full replay remain future work.
The world controller polls authoritative jobs as physical state; it does not call
another agent to complete work. Evaluated agents communicate through events only.

# Multi-basket fleet and judged recovery

The fixed `delivery delivery-demo` runs the local 32×32 synthetic scenario below.
The grid UI is retired; [configurable running-city sessions](RUNNING-CITY.md) remain
as backend regressions, with saved fixed runs inspectable through the delivery API.
Existing saved 10×10 runs and the separate `/lab` inventory
crash/replenishment exercise retain their earlier behavior.

The expanded city has 1,024 nodes, 3,968 directed adjacent roads and 12 establishments:
six supermarkets, three retail stores and three pharmacies. Pharmacy catalogue
rows are simulated hygiene goods. They contain no patient, prescription or medical
decision data. Opening inventory is one or two units per stocked product.

## What the seeded scenario demonstrates

Seven one-item basket requests compete for stock and four bike couriers. Three
couriers start online; the fourth becomes available as a replacement at simulation
second 180. Two baskets compete for the same last unit, so one is rejected. Six
parcels are picked exactly once.

Persistent seeded congestion doubles every directed road's traversal time.
Route validation and physical motion use the same per-edge durations. At second
180 two couriers suffer simulated mechanical failures. Each parcel stays at the
last reached safe checkpoint. A replacement must travel there and collect it;
the system never returns it to a store or consumes another stock unit.

For seed 42, the judge approves recovery of `delivery-a` and denies `delivery-b`,
whose deliberately tight delivery window has already expired. The approved parcel
receives attempt two and a new courier. The final result is five delivered baskets,
one abandoned parcel held at its checkpoint and one rejected stock request.
Abandoned is an explicit failure outcome, not a successful delivery or vanished stock.

## The call is a queued briefing

This demo simulates the call with a scoped queued message. It makes no telephone,
voice-provider or model calls. Dispatch sends `courier.briefed`; the selected courier
agent reads its current briefing and sends `courier.accepted`. Physical departure
cannot precede acknowledgement. If acknowledgement is delayed, departure, pickup
and arrival times move together rather than inventing travel during that delay.

Recovery follows this queue and physical-custody boundary. The fixed scenario
uses local rules. A separately enabled judge can consume a saved provider verdict
through the [durable inference protocol](DURABLE-INFERENCE.md); the same execution
gates remain in force.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Review["01 / Judge review"]
        Failure["World failure: parcel retained at safe checkpoint"]
        Candidate["Scoped judge computes local courier and route candidate"]
        Verdict["Local rules or saved optional provider verdict; SQL persists bounded review"]
        Failure -->|"Queued delivery.failed"| Candidate
        Candidate --> Verdict
    end
    subgraph Decision["02 / Dispatcher decision"]
        Apply["Apply matching current-attempt review"]
        Held["Denied: abandoned; parcel stays at checkpoint"]
        Retry["Queued dispatch.retry; wait if fleet is busy"]
        Gate["Fresh SQL checks: approved review, free online courier, route, deadline and retry limits"]
        Apply -->|"Denied"| Held
        Apply -->|"Approved"| Retry
        Retry --> Gate
    end
    subgraph Movement["03 / Physical handoff"]
        Assign["Atomic new attempt, courier assignment and scoped briefing"]
        Accept["Queued courier.briefed and courier.accepted before departure"]
        Travel["Collect same parcel at checkpoint; world records delivery.arrived"]
        Complete["Dispatcher confirms delivery.completed"]
        Assign --> Accept --> Travel --> Complete
    end
    Verdict -->|"Queued recovery.reviewed"| Apply
    Gate -->|"All checks pass"| Assign
```

All role-to-role handoffs use the durable event queue. A self-queued dispatch retry
waits when all online couriers are busy. No role directly calls another role.
The trusted scheduler activates only the appropriate authenticated worker; it does
not pass the operator snapshot into an agent.

## Relevant memory without sharing private memory

A recovery brief is an immutable, run/basket/attempt-scoped export of canonical
facts: objective, custody checkpoint, customer node, prior courier/attempt, failure
reason, source event references, judge verdict, deadline and route. It contains
neither product/price information nor another agent's private episodes, soul or
transcript. The selected courier can read its own current brief; another courier
cannot retrieve or accept it. Old attempt messages cannot mutate the replacement
attempt.

Private expiring agent memory remains in its existing authenticated namespace.
Shared briefs, incidents and reviews are separate operator-owned records accessed
through narrow role projections. An exported brief does not grant access to the
source event bodies or the source agent's memory.

## Judge and permission gates

The judge is a deterministic operational role, distinct from a future external eval
scorer. It sees the failed logistics job, current custody, available online couriers
and traffic-adjusted roads. It cannot inspect stock or product data, assign couriers,
move parcels or confirm delivery.

The database independently recomputes the proposed route. A retry needs an online
free courier, a matching current-attempt review, enough remaining deadline, fewer
than two total attempts, and at most 100 simulated route-minutes. Dispatch rechecks
these limits at assignment time. A prompt or forged verdict event cannot replace
the persisted review. Route-minutes are a synthetic retry-cost proxy, not money.

Thirty independently scoped logins cover 12 inventory roles, 12 fulfillment roles,
four courier roles, one dispatcher and one judge. Courier and judge logins cannot
read raw operational tables or execute another role's commands. Legacy command entry points cannot be called by agents to bypass the expanded checks. The host, fixed Python policy
code and operator interface remain trusted; arbitrary agent-written Python is not
sandboxed by these database boundaries.

Dispatcher limits are explicitly configured at 150 attempts and 1,200 reserved
tool slots for the larger scenario. Other role defaults remain 100 attempts and
400 slots. The aggregate cap remains 500 attempts and 2,000 slots; model caps remain
zero. Durable reservations are not refunded on crashes or replayed attempts.

## Evidence and current limits

The inspector exposes current routes, online/offline fleet state, traffic and dropout
incidents, judge reasons, custody briefs, attempt history, budgets and event lineage.
Arrival/collection timeline entries come from recorded physical observations, not
obsolete planned timestamps. Evidence exports retain checkpoints and conserved stock.

The full Linux suite passes **86 tests**, Ruff and mypy. Chrome checks pass for
city counts, both judge verdicts, custody briefing provenance, evidence download,
completed-run reload and desktop/mobile layout.

Verification covers two independent dispatcher workers claiming different queued
jobs while competing for one online bike: one assigns, the other defers. It also
covers cross-courier briefing denial, cross-role command denial, missing-review
denial, acknowledgement timing, stock conservation, custody tracking and both judge
outcomes. Existing Madrid, inventory crash and legacy delivery tests remain part
of the regression suite.

Freshly published events are immediately wall-clock eligible; simulation due time
still controls scheduling. Wall-clock retry backoff and leases remain enforced.
This prevents transaction timestamps or clock adjustments from making fresh events
temporarily invisible and changing a seeded run's initial assignments.

Still deferred for this fixed scenario: real voice calls, live traffic, arbitrary incidents,
road-capacity queues, cargo/energy constraints, cancellation/returns, controller
restart recovery, full replay and published multi-seed architecture comparisons.

# Configurable local city sessions

The Delivery workspace and its 32×32 grid-city screen are retired. Use Operations
at `/` for the Madrid map and fleets; `/delivery-lab` redirects there. This document
records the retained running-city backend and the former controls. Configure a
session with `POST /api/lab/city-runs`, inspect its state with
`GET /api/lab/delivery-runs/{run}`, and inspect a scoped agent with
`GET /api/lab/city-runs/{run}/agents/{agent_id}`. These runs are separate from Madrid.

## Controls

| Control | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Store name / open for orders | Rename or enable any of the 12 establishments for the next session |
| Stock units | Opening units **per product** at that store, from 0 to 20 |
| Store couriers | 0–3 home couriers per enabled store, with at most 16 in the city |
| Store demand weight | Relative share of arriving orders, from 0 to 3; zero receives no demand |
| Orders per hour | Total city arrival intensity, from 0 to 24; not a rate per shop |
| Duration | Demand generation for 15–120 simulated minutes |
| Traffic multiplier | 0.5–3 times each directed road's base traversal time |
| Dropout / courier-hour | Withdrawal intensity from 0 to 1 per courier-hour |
| Seed | Reproduce the generated demand and withdrawal schedule for the same settings |
| Playback | Target wall-clock playback duration; local processing can extend it |

Settings are frozen at session creation. Saving changes while observing a run edits
the next-run draft, not the current city's stock or history. The persisted configuration
and its hash accompany the run's evidence. Shop positions and categories use the
fixed 12-establishment layout; adding arbitrary map locations is future work.

A store's courier team is a home/employer relationship. Dispatch can send available
couriers from other stores. That relationship grants no inventory or colleague-memory
access: each courier still sees only its own current job and briefing.

## Demand and physical behavior

Orders use seeded exponential interarrival times. Enabled stores are sampled by
their demand weights; products and customer grid nodes are sampled locally. Requests
are released into the queue only when their simulation arrival time is reached.
Future order schedules are operator evidence, not an agent observation or pre-created
fulfillment task. Release is idempotent. Insufficient stock produces real rejections.

Each courier has a seeded first withdrawal time derived from the configured hourly
intensity. Zero disables withdrawal. An idle withdrawal makes the courier unavailable;
an active failure retains parcel custody and queues the existing judge/recovery flow.
No fixed second-180 dropout or forced standby courier is used in configured sessions.

Traffic scales road travel time consistently in planning, independent command
validation and physical motion. Fractional edge times are rounded up individually.
The traffic configuration is read from trusted persisted state, not a model proposal.

Sessions admit at most 24 arrivals, then allow a 60-minute simulated drain after the
demand window. They are finite observations, not perpetual city services. Remaining
jobs stay visible as unfinished when the window ends. If a durable agent/run budget
is exhausted, the session stops with a budget-limit summary and preserves pending
work; it does not turn it into successful deliveries. Existing caps and zero model
spend remain enforced.

## Agent inspection and isolation

Shop panels separate overview, stock and team. An agent panel shows relevant store,
traffic or risk parameters, resource budgets, live private memory and its own courier
briefings. Role definitions/tools are available under details. Memory carries observed
time, expiry and source event; expired entries are counted separately and excluded
from the current-memory list. Refresh the panel to inspect the latest state.

This is a **human operator** view. Its endpoint resolves a requested agent inside
one run, then filters memory by that binding's authenticated namespace. It never
returns login credentials or passes the human inspector into another agent's context.
Database roles, scoped commands and queue-only communication remain unchanged.
The configuration table has no raw agent grants. Home-store staffing does not broaden
an agent's role permissions.

## Verification

The original running-city release passed **91 tests**, Ruff and mypy. Coverage includes settings
limits, repeatable demand, timed/idempotent release, configured stock/staffing,
fractional traffic recomputation, immutable run settings and selected-agent memory
isolation, plus the existing fleet, crash and Madrid regressions.

The obsolete grid browser smoke scripts have been removed. Backend regressions
remain in `tests/test_running_city.py`, `tests/test_delivery_api.py` and the fleet
suite. The fixed `delivery delivery-demo` remains the deterministic recovery
regression documented in [fleet recovery](FLEET-RECOVERY.md). Controller restart
recovery, arbitrary stores and longer continuous services remain deferred.

## Households, assortment and streets

New sessions use 128 synthetic households with stable IDs, addresses and homes.
Search a household or select its house to inspect upcoming, active and past orders
within the session. These are seeded simulated arrivals, not predictions or promises.
Entity filters switch between shops, customers and couriers. Stock views show product
names and SKUs: 60 grocery products per supermarket and 30 per retail/pharmacy shop
(120 distinct products across the city). Pharmacy products are hygiene goods.

The city has nine neighborhoods, residential blocks, offices and parks. Alternating
interior streets are one-way; perimeter roads are two-way. The 2,108 directed road
edges remain strongly connected. Couriers plan and travel on those actual edges.
Existing fixed chaos runs retain their original regression graph.

## What the agents actually do

These delivery-lab agents are deterministic Python workers. They do not use an AI
key, call a model or perform AI reasoning. Role definitions and SOUL files describe
and version each identity; current policies do not ask a model to interpret them.
Inventory reserves stock, fulfillment picks it, dispatch assigns routes, couriers
move orders, and a rule-based judge gates recovery after a dropout.

The foundation enforces scoped database identities, tools, private memory, budgets
and queued communication. It demonstrates these controls and recovery behavior,
not LLM judgement or learned behavior. Household profiles and future schedules are
operator views; agent projections expose only the role's required operational data.
Any future model adapter needs separate evaluation before claiming AI capability.

## Courier traces

Route colors distinguish couriers. Solid faded sections show travelled distance;
dashed sections show the remaining plan, and a diamond marks the destination.
A route can revisit a junction while approaching a shop and then delivering.
Couriers move only after accepting an assignment, using each persisted road
duration. Selecting a shop or order can expose its route for inspection.

## Appearance and fictional team names

The madrid-delivery-sim interface uses a dark operations palette: blue-tinted surfaces,
red brand accent, blue controls and bordered panels. Fonts use local system fallbacks
when Space Grotesk/Space Mono are unavailable; no remote font requests are made.
Map shops, household icons and couriers are enlarged for easier selection.

Agents have stable fictional display names, such as Lucia Rios (inventory),
Lucia Luna (fulfillment), Lucia Mora (courier), Elena Vega (dispatcher), and
Victor Sol (judge). Names are presentation labels; role IDs, queue destinations,
database permissions and memory namespaces keep their original identities.

## Operations workspace

The overview pairs the dispatch map with session metrics and a contextual inspector.
Metrics show order volume, active deliveries, delivered orders, available couriers
and job exceptions from the saved run. Network activity lists recorded incidents.
The order book filters all, active or attention-required orders; selecting an order
opens its household context and route when that run contains household metadata.
Fleet opens named courier cards and their scoped inspectors. Stores opens the
establishment directory and shop controls. The Overview navigation returns to the
operations watch. These views are operator projections, not additional agent access.

## Live movement and driver inspection

New sessions default to a 90-second playback. Courier markers interpolate along
accepted route edges between authoritative snapshots and stop at the latest
received simulation time; the browser does not invent future movement. Instant
playback remains available. The order book admits arrivals over simulated time,
with a brief new-order notice; future household schedules remain inspectable.

Select a courier to see the fictional name, current order, pickup/drop-off,
remaining ETA in simulated minutes/seconds, route focus and that courier's private
memory. Active courier memory refreshes while observed. ETA includes persisted
traffic-adjusted road durations and is frozen when the simulation stops.

The optional GCP recovery-judge switch applies to the next session. It stays
unavailable until a server-owned gateway and keyless caller identity are configured.
See [GCP deployment and teardown](GCP-AI.md). The city and routine workers stay local.

# Dispatch from the street

The Madrid map now defaults to rolling maximum-cardinality, minimum-cost
assignment. Couriers start across nearby stores and remain at their last drop-off
until another job is assigned. A home-base label is administrative affiliation,
not a return instruction. Everything runs locally without model calls.

## What was wrong

The previous dispatcher minimized completion ETA and broke ties by courier ID.
Food preparation can make several completion ETAs identical: the nearby courier
waits longer at the restaurant, while a farther courier spends that time driving.
The lexical tie then selects `01`, even though it wastes empty kilometres.

The backend already retained the customer's node after delivery. The apparent
return on the map came from resetting animation on duplicate snapshots: the UI
projected movement ahead, then drew the same older position again. Six couriers
also began at each hub, obscuring individual markers. One monotonic display clock
now supplies both rendering and animation; duplicate polls do not reset it.
Projection remains bounded to one 60-second simulation tick. SQL snapshots use a
short, read-only repeatable-read transaction so clock, routes and positions agree.

## Assignment algorithm

At each queue-triggered dispatch opportunity, the dispatcher reads at most 100
pending orders and 100 eligible idle couriers. Arrivals already share the city's
60-second clock; no extra artificial batching delay is introduced.

1. Construct directed road routes from each courier's **current** node, through
   the store, to the customer. Never substitute the home-base node.
2. Exclude unreachable routes, insufficient energy reserves and shift overruns.
3. Solve the feasible bipartite graph with exact maximum flow and minimum cost.
   First maximize served orders; then prioritize the earliest deadlines; then
   minimize economic cost for that served order set. Each courier and order may
   participate in one assignment. Charging lateness only to selected jobs would
   otherwise make an overdue order increasingly unattractive when capacity is
   tight. Bounded binary priority weights prevent that starvation trap.
4. For equal total economic cost, prefer longer-idle couriers, then fewer completed
   jobs, then a seeded, non-lexical tie. Fairness does not override road economics.
5. Commit reservations, decision evidence, the queue handoff and event ACK
   atomically. The existing active-order uniqueness constraint still protects
   against competing dispatchers. Couriers accept work through the queue.

The score uses generalized seconds:

```text
completion_duration
+ 20 × lateness
+ empty_pickup_travel_time
+ marginal_vehicle_cost × 3600 / 12
```

The €12/hour conversion, lateness and empty-time weights are editable in the
validated `dispatch` object on `POST /api/runs`. Each run stores a frozen policy.
The UI exposes the two main choices: economic versus legacy dispatch, and staying
at drop-off versus experimental demand-aware repositioning. The legacy arm keeps
the original earliest-completion/ID rule for controlled comparisons. Historical
runs with no policy retain their original interpretation.

Each assignment records its source node, pickup distance, ETA, cost components,
eligible count, batch size and up to five alternative courier scores. An
individually second-best match can be selected when it improves the whole batch.
Inspect this under a courier's recorded evidence on the map.

## Empty travel costs something

Actual movement updates distance, empty distance, normalized energy and marginal
operating cost every tick, including unfinished trips. Cumulative per-leg meters
make repeated ticks and crash replay idempotent. Preparation waits add no distance.
A completed delivery adds the existing €1 task fee once.

| Vehicle | Synthetic marginal cost | Normalized energy per km |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Bike | €0.12/km | 1.5 |
| Moto | €0.28/km | 0.7 |
| Van | €0.55/km | 0.4 |

These are simulation assumptions, not measured fuel prices or driver pay. Time
has value in the optimization objective; hourly wages are not charged in the
operating-cost ledger. Whole-fleet cost per completed delivery includes actual
empty repositioning and partial travel. Historical runs predate these meters:
their original completed-task cost remains an estimate and missing empty meters
are displayed as unavailable rather than zero.

## Repositioning is optional and conservative

**Stay at drop-off is the default.** The experimental alternative uses only orders
observed within the previous 30 minutes. It estimates next-15-minute demand,
checks the coverage supplied by other idle couriers and already reserved
destinations, and proposes a move only when the estimated reduction in pickup
time exceeds travel expense plus a two-minute margin.

Moves have a distance cap, cooldown, energy reserve and shift/run horizon. At
most two are proposed per event, and none while orders are still pending. A
durable `courier.reposition` event must be acknowledged before movement begins.
Delayed handoffs rebase departure to acceptance time or cancel when the move no
longer fits. Ordinary delivery assignments also rebase departure and remaining
preparation wait; an infeasible acceptance releases the order for a fresh,
versioned assignment. Every metre consumes energy and cost. There is no teleport or
automatic hub return. Stores with fewer than two observed orders are not targets.

Coverage treats another moving courier's reserved destination as future supply;
this simple forecast can be wrong. Repositioning can cost more than waiting. It
stays optional and is evaluated separately rather than advertised as an automatic
improvement.

## Two city runtimes, explicit boundaries

| Runtime | Implemented here | Remaining work |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Madrid baseline (`/`) | Fleet batch optimization, marginal economics, distributed starts, optional real repositioning, monotonic movement | Traffic-dependent ETA, mode-specific access, bundled multi-stop trips, reassignment during empty travel, calibrated costs and demand forecasting |
| Restaurant/delivery labs | Shared matching primitive for the one basket visible to the role; directed traffic-weighted routes; actual live/custody node; stable basket-specific ties; common-leg search reuse | A scoped multi-order projection and economics ledger before fleet-wide batching/repositioning |

The lab change does not grant access to raw fleet, jobs or another agent's memory.
Its planner receives the existing authorized projection. A global restaurant
optimizer needs a separately reviewed projection/tool, not broader SQL grants.
The Madrid graph still uses fixed mode speeds and a shared directed drivable
network; the lab's simulated traffic weights are not silently applied to it.
Soft lateness penalties do not guarantee every deadline under overloaded demand.
The bounded pending window takes the first 100 deadlines. A backlog of 100
infeasible orders can hide feasible later orders; paged candidate search and an
explicit unsatisfiable-order policy remain future work.

## Reproduce and inspect

Run only against the dedicated local test database. No provider keys or cloud
credentials are needed:

```bash
docker compose exec -T app python scripts/benchmark_dispatch.py \
  --seed 42 --seed 73 --include-reposition \
  --output artifacts/dispatch-comparison.json
node --test scripts/test_courier_motion.cjs
docker compose exec -T app python -m pytest \
  tests/test_dispatch_optimizer.py tests/test_workflow_dispatch.py \
  tests/test_economic_dispatch.py
```

The comparison pairs the same graph, initial fleet and seeded demand; it clears
the route cache between arms and saves complete snapshots. Its wall time includes
SQL, queue handling and Python overhead; it is not a solver-only latency claim.
Costs and job spread accompany completion and lateness so an apparent saving
cannot hide dropped work. The two seeded days are examples, not a statistical
claim about production performance. See the committed [comparison receipt](evidence/dispatch-comparison.json).

Final-policy results on the pinned road graph:

| Seed | Policy | On time / orders | Empty km | Operating cost | Jobs per courier |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 42 | Legacy, stay | 247 / 247 | 336.980 | €453.96 | 2–35 |
| 42 | Deadline + cost, stay | 247 / 247 | 253.930 | €391.52 | 4–22 |
| 42 | Deadline + cost, reposition | 247 / 247 | 267.316 | €400.76 | 5–22 |
| 73 | Legacy, stay | 248 / 248 | 357.692 | €470.45 | 0–37 |
| 73 | Deadline + cost, stay | 248 / 248 | 260.721 | €401.38 | 5–24 |
| 73 | Deadline + cost, reposition | 248 / 248 | 279.793 | €410.09 | 6–24 |

Across both days, staying with the new matcher reduces empty travel by 25.915%
and simulated total operating cost by 14.227%, with all 495 deliveries on time
and zero dead letters. Repositioning adds 87.376 km of movement and costs more
than staying on these days, which supports keeping it optional. No paid calls
were made. The receipt's source hash matches the final dispatch code; an earlier
exploratory run was superseded after the deadline and handoff fixes.

Tests cover exhaustive small-graph assignment oracles, a greedy assignment trap,
input permutations, bounded batches, equal-ETA near/far regression, staying at
drop-off, partial and duplicate ticks, waiting, one completion fee, delayed/cancelled
relocation, observed-only history, distance/energy/horizon bounds, scoped lab
traffic routes and the animation rewind. Python cases appear under City &
fulfillment in `/health`; the six Node movement cases also run in CI.
The full local suite passed 704 Python tests, Ruff, mypy over 57 modules, twelve
agent scenarios repeated twice with matching business outcomes, and six offline
judge cases. HTTP checks verified local assets and control bindings. A browser
visual review was unavailable because the computer-use service exposed no browsers.

## Why this approach

Uber publicly describes matching nearby requests in short batches to reduce
collective waiting rather than immediately selecting the nearest driver. Its
older Eats engineering account also explains why preparation time and pickup
waiting matter. This project adopts those public principles with an inspectable
operations-research algorithm. It does not reproduce Uber's private production
model or claim state-of-the-art delivery performance. Research on dynamic pickup
and delivery also studies reoptimization with travel and tardiness costs; learned
lookahead and multi-stop search are future extensions here.

Sources reviewed 2026-10-29: [Uber matching](https://www.uber.com/au/en/marketplace/matching/),
[Uber Eats trip optimization (2018)](https://www.uber.com/us/en/blog/uber-eats-trip-optimization/),
[dynamic pickup/delivery cost approximation research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.01915).

Implementation: [matcher](../src/delivery/dispatch_optimizer.py),
[policy](../src/delivery/dispatch_policy.py),
[dispatcher and courier](../src/delivery/agents.py),
[repositioning](../src/delivery/dispatch_reposition.py),
[scoped lab planner](../src/delivery/workflow_policy.py),
[road geometry and progress](../src/delivery/world.py),
[snapshot and initial fleet](../src/delivery/simulation.py),
[migration](../sql/migrations/027_economic_dispatch.sql),
[comparison script](../scripts/benchmark_dispatch.py),
[matcher tests](../tests/test_dispatch_optimizer.py),
[economics and recovery tests](../tests/test_economic_dispatch.py),
[lab planner tests](../tests/test_workflow_dispatch.py).

# GCP components: exact implementation and ownership

Source review: 2026-10-28. These are the resources and call paths defined by this
repository. No cloud resources were started or queried for this documentation
change. Last live lifecycle evidence is dated 2026-10-25 in
[GCP verification](GCP-VERIFICATION.md): the dedicated project was ACTIVE, billing
disabled and billable demo runtime removed. Run the documented status command to
check a later session; do not treat a source review as a fresh cloud inventory.

## Architecture as built

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Local[Local Docker environment]
        UI[Operator UI and trusted controller]
        Agents[Scoped Python role workers]
        DB[(Postgres: domain state, queue, memory, budgets, audit)]
        Caller[CloudJudge client and caller ID token]
        UI --> Agents
        Agents <--> DB
        Agents -->|Optional judge policy only| Caller
    end
    subgraph GCP[Dedicated Terraform-owned GCP project]
        IAM[Cloud Run IAM invocation check]
        Gateway[Cloud Run judgement service]
        Vertex[Google publisher model through Vertex REST]
        Registry[Artifact Registry: pinned gateway image]
        Logs[Platform logs and structured gateway stdout]
        IAM --> Gateway
        Registry -.-> Gateway
        Gateway -->|Runtime service account ADC| Vertex
        Gateway --> Logs
    end
    Caller -->|HTTPS and audience-bound ID token| IAM
    Gateway -->|Schema-validated verdict and usage| Caller
```

Inventory, restaurants, dispatch, courier motion, canonical memory and the durable
queue run locally. Redis is a local baseline support service; it is not the
authoritative agent transport. There is no Cloud SQL, Pub/Sub, GKE, managed agent
runtime, managed Memory Bank or ADK deployment in this Terraform root.

## Terraform resource inventory

[main.tf](../infra/gcp-ai/main.tf) is the only cloud infrastructure root for this
demo. It requires Terraform 1.6+ and Google provider `~> 7.0`; the committed provider
lock file resolves an exact selected build. State is local to this root and ignored
by Git. Scrapmarket's project, backend and credentials are not imported or reused.

| Terraform address | Purpose and actual configuration | Retained when parked? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `google_project.ai` | Dedicated project; no default network; application labels; `deletion_policy=PREVENT` and `prevent_destroy=true` | Yes |
| `google_project_service.api["run.googleapis.com"]` | Cloud Run administration API | Yes |
| `google_project_service.api["artifactregistry.googleapis.com"]` | Container repository API | Yes |
| `google_project_service.api["aiplatform.googleapis.com"]` | Google model inference/token-counting API | Yes |
| `google_project_service.api["iam.googleapis.com"]` | Service-account/role administration | Yes |
| `google_project_service.api["iamcredentials.googleapis.com"]` | Short-lived impersonated credentials | Yes |
| `google_project_service.api["cloudresourcemanager.googleapis.com"]` | Project lifecycle/metadata | Yes |
| `google_service_account.judge[0]` | `judgement-runtime`, attached to the Cloud Run service | Yes |
| `google_project_iam_custom_role.judge_predict[0]` | `boundedJudgePredict`: only `aiplatform.endpoints.predict` | Yes |
| `google_project_iam_member.vertex[0]` | Grants that custom prediction role to the runtime account | Yes |
| `google_service_account.caller[0]` | `judgement-caller`, separate invocation identity | Yes |
| `google_service_account_iam_binding.caller_tokens[0]` | Explicit operator/service principals may impersonate the caller via `roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator` | Yes |
| `google_artifact_registry_repository.images[0]` | Regional Docker repository `judgement`; image storage can cost money | No |
| `google_cloud_run_v2_service.judge[0]` | Regional stateless `judgement` endpoint | No |
| `google_cloud_run_v2_service_iam_binding.invoker[0]` | Only the caller service account receives this service's `roles/run.invoker` binding | No |

That is **12 retained foundation resources**, plus **3 runtime resources** when
fully enabled. Provider-managed service agents, service revisions and platform
audit records are not independent resources declared in this root. The project
IAM binding is additive; the service-account/service bindings are authoritative
for their respective roles. Shared-project IAM must not be managed accidentally.

The invoker member validation accepts explicit user/service-account principals,
not public principals. The current Cloud Run setting is nevertheless
`INGRESS_TRAFFIC_ALL`: the HTTPS endpoint is network-reachable, with IAM protecting
invocation. **Authenticated invocation is not private network ingress.** There is
no VPC, IAP front end, Agent Gateway or Model Armor resource in the deployed module.

## Service sizing, build and model configuration

| Setting | Current code |
| --- | --- |
| Container | Python 3.12 slim, locked Python dependencies, FastAPI/Uvicorn, UID/GID 65532 |
| Contents | Gateway source, meal-snapshot validator and synthetic `data/meal-snapshot.json`; no database exports or agent credentials |
| Build | Local Docker `linux/amd64` build; no Cloud Build job or staging bucket |
| Image | Local push to Artifact Registry; lifecycle helper verifies a single repository digest and deploys the immutable `@sha256` reference |
| CPU / memory | 1 vCPU / 512 MiB; request-based CPU allocation, startup boost off |
| Scaling | Service and template minimum 0, maximum 1; concurrency 4 |
| Request timeout | Cloud Run 35 seconds; local caller 30 seconds |
| Gateway input/output | Strict Pydantic objects; 8,192-byte assembled request bound; 256 maximum output tokens; bounded response reads |
| Vertex transport | REST `:countTokens` followed by `:generateContent`, authenticated using runtime ADC |
| Token/request timing | Token count timeout 5 seconds, generation request timeout 15 seconds; successful response usage is checked |
| Thinking / output | `MINIMAL`, JSON MIME type, two-decision response schema; these settings require a compatible model |
| Runtime environment | `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT`, `VERTEX_REGION`, `VERTEX_MODEL` |

Sources are [Dockerfile](../infra/gcp-ai/Dockerfile),
[gateway.py](../infra/gcp-ai/gateway.py),
[variables.tf](../infra/gcp-ai/variables.tf) and
[gcp_demo.py](../scripts/gcp_demo.py). Terraform requires explicit region, model
location and model identifier; this documentation does not read private variable
files. Historically verified values were Cloud Run `europe-west1`, Vertex
`global`, and `gemini-3.5-flash-lite`. That deployment is **not** an EU-only
inference processing claim. Returned model version and gateway revision are more
useful experiment provenance than a model-family label alone.

Zero minimum instances is a demo cost/latency choice, not an availability SLO or
guarantee of no storage/logging/inference charges. Configured maximum instances
and concurrency constrain capacity, not total spend. See
[Cloud Run billing behavior](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/configuring/billing-settings).

## Authentication, step by step

1. An explicitly cloud-enabled local run freezes its gateway origin. Base Compose
   does not mount cloud credentials. The opt-in
   [Compose override](../compose.gcp-ai.yaml) mounts the operator's ADC directory
   read-only; it is never copied into an image or Git.
2. `identity_token` in [cloud_ai.py](../src/delivery/cloud_ai.py) uses ADC to
   impersonate `judgement-caller`, obtaining an ID token whose audience is the
   gateway service origin. The client accepts only a Cloud Run HTTPS origin.
3. Cloud Run checks that token and its service-level invocation policy before
   FastAPI handles `/judge`. The application relies on this platform authentication;
   it does not independently validate arbitrary JWTs or enforce per-tenant quotas.
4. Cloud Run executes as `judgement-runtime`. Runtime ADC provides OAuth access
   to the Google publisher model through its prediction-only custom role. No
   downloaded service-account key or model API key is needed.
5. The cloud runtime has no simulation database connection or business action
   tools. It returns a verdict; local SQL still decides whether any retry is legal.

The custom role is prediction-only at **project** scope, not an IAM allowlist for
one model ID. The configured model is an application-controlled selection. The
caller impersonation role can mint more than ID tokens; a client deployment should
test whether its actual flow can use a narrower grant. Neither current account is
a managed Agent Identity with runtime-bound agent credentials.

This follows the distinction between caller ID tokens and runtime service identity
in Google's [authenticated invocation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/authenticating/service-to-service)
and [service identity](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/configuring/services/service-identity)
guides. Local ADC is a development credential flow. Enterprise CI should use
restricted Workload Identity Federation, not a copied user ADC file.

## Exactly what reaches the model

`sanitized_request` permits finite numeric values for `attempt`, `retry_limit`,
`deadline_sim`, `sim_time` and optional `cost_eur`; a candidate contains only
`estimated_seconds`, `remaining_seconds` and `route_nodes`. It sends the number
of recalled entries, capped at 100, **not their bodies**. Customer names, order IDs,
courier IDs, route coordinates, local SOUL and private Bakiano rows are omitted.

The gateway adds its packaged seven-meal, seventeen-ingredient, three-fictional-
market snapshot. Its fixed prompt permits only `approve_retry` or `deny_retry`
with a short reason; it exposes no tools. Snapshot and prompt versions are logged.
This is read-only reference for pizza, kebab, hamburgers, steak frites, sushi, soups
and salads; the judge does not procure ingredients or substitute a meal.

Before inference, deterministic preflight denies absent/invalid numeric facts,
missing candidates, exhausted retries and infeasible deadlines/route duration.
The 6,000-second route threshold is a simulation step/duration bound, **not a GCP
monetary budget**. A JSON-conforming answer is still subject to local feasibility
and custody checks. Authentication, transport or validation failure denies the
AI-enabled retry. No silent switch to local approval is made within that run.

The configured cumulative allowance is six calls/50,688 tokens per run. Each
newly dispatched request reserves 8,448 tokens; saved-result replay does not reserve
another call. The whole allowance is not
reserved upfront. This does not enforce a project-wide currency budget,
block another authorized direct caller, or guarantee exactly-once model billing.
The local judge adapter now commits a request and dispatch marker, closes its
database connection for remote I/O, saves the result and applies it in a fresh
fenced transaction. Reclaimed events reuse completed results; uncertain abandoned
invocations fail closed without automatic resend. This changes local orchestration,
not the deployed Terraform resource inventory. See [durable inference](DURABLE-INFERENCE.md).

## Observability and its current limits

Gateway structured stdout records event class, decision, prompt version, snapshot
hash, Cloud Run revision and, for actual model answers, model version, token usage
and elapsed milliseconds. Preflight denials record zero model tokens. Local model
audit records attach provider/verdict/usage/error class to the event attempt.

Platform request/audit logging and gateway stdout are available, but Terraform does
not configure custom log retention, dashboards, alert policies, Cloud Trace spans
or OpenTelemetry export. There is no complete distributed trace from the local
order through Cloud Run/Vertex: correlation IDs are deliberately excluded from the
model body, and a separate sanitized tracing propagation channel remains to be
added. Do not describe the local event inspector as deployed Cloud Trace or as
access to a model's private reasoning.

## Start, inspect and park

These are operational commands, **not steps required to read this documentation**:

```bash
make gcp-start
make gcp-status
make gcp-stop
```

`start` verifies prerequisites, links billing with runtime enabled/gateway disabled,
builds/pushes the image, then deploys the gateway and reconnects the local app.
It enables the UI option but does not select it or initiate inference. `status`
reads project/billing/service/state information and never links billing merely to
inspect Artifact Registry. That check is reported unavailable when billing is off.

`stop` first attempts to restore base local Compose, then removes the service,
invoker binding and image repository **while billing is still linked**. A second
Terraform apply unlinks billing. Project, APIs and IAM identities remain. The helper
validates saved plans against phase-specific resource/project allowlists and uses
a local lifecycle lock. Shutdown failure is explicit; it is not reported as parked.

Ordinary `terraform destroy` is intentionally blocked by project protection.
This implements the later requirement to preserve project/IAM between sessions.
Full project erasure is a separate reviewed lifecycle change, not the daily stop
command. Prior invoices, delayed usage reporting and retained platform audit
records are not erased. The helper controls this root's resources, not arbitrary
resources created manually or in another project.

Cloud SQL, remote Terraform state buckets, secrets, managed memory, traces and any
future paid service must have an explicit owner, Terraform coverage and stop/data-
retention policy before adoption. A production retention requirement can introduce
an intentional cost floor; it must never be advertised as a free parked demo.
See [the complete operations runbook](GCP-AI.md).
